title: Framework Deal with Lebanon Divides Israel as Hezbollah Rejects Terms
summary: A framework agreement signed Friday by Israel, Lebanon, and the United States has sparked cautious optimism in Israel but outright rejection from Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group that controls much of southern Lebanon. The deal, negotiated in Washington, outlines a “sequenced process”: the Lebanese army must restore authority over all Lebanese territory and verify the disarmament of non-state armed groups—a clear reference to Hezbollah—before Israeli forces can “progressively redeploy” from areas they’ve occupied since a renewed offensive in March. That offensive has killed more than 4,000 people. The framework does not specify how disarmament will be verified, but it establishes two “pilot zones” for an initial Israeli withdrawal where the Lebanese military will assume security responsibility. Hezbollah’s Secretary-General Naim Qassem swiftly rejected the agreement as “null and void,” insisting that a separate Iran-U.S. memorandum of understanding should be the basis for ending the conflict. He warned that linking Israel’s withdrawal to Hezbollah’s disarmament crossed “all red lines.” In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu framed the deal as a strategic victory, telling the public it deals a major blow to Iran and ensures Israel maintains a buffer zone until Hezbollah is disarmed. “Iran is trying to coax us to withdraw from southern Lebanon by force,” he said. “Israel, Lebanon and the United States are telling Iran—it is none of your business.” However, opposition leader Yair Lapid criticized the framework, arguing it allows Iran to continue funding Hezbollah. Former Deputy Prime Minister Avigdor Lieberman warned that as long as Hezbollah exists, “the next confrontation is only a matter of time.” Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s principal challenger, said Israel “failed to capitalise on our military achievements.” Local leaders in northern Israel, the region most exposed to Hezbollah attacks, reacted with guarded hope. David Azoulay, head of the Metula Regional Council, welcomed the deal but stressed that any withdrawal must remain conditional and carefully managed. Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, summed up the uncertainty: “Only time and its implementation will determine whether this is a real agreement or just something signed.”
why_it_matters: The clash between a state, a non‑state militant group, and a foreign power like Iran shows how messy modern conflicts can be—and why agreements often fail. For teenagers watching the news, this case teaches that disarmament and peace depend not just on signatures, but on trust, verification, and all sides accepting limits, which can shape their understanding of international crises and the role of diplomacy in their own future.

background_read: Hezbollah is a Shiite militant group and political party in Lebanon, backed by Iran, that has fought multiple wars with Israel since the 1980s. Southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah holds great influence, has been a flashpoint for decades, and a 2006 war ended with UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which called for the disarming of all militias in Lebanon—a promise that was never fulfilled. In the article, the framework agreement is the latest attempt to break this cycle after a renewed Israeli offensive in March killed over 4,000 people and led to Israeli troops occupying areas near the border.

The deal brings together key leaders: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s Prime Minister since 2022, who has long warned about Iran’s influence through Hezbollah; Naim Qassem, who became Hezbollah’s Secretary-General after the killing of Hassan Nasrallah in 2023; and Yair Lapid, head of the Israeli opposition and a former prime minister. The Metula Regional Council, mentioned by David Azoulay, represents a northern Israeli town that has endured constant rocket fire from Lebanon. Chatham House, the think tank where Yossi Mekelberg works, is a leading UK-based institute that studies international affairs and Middle East conflict.

perspectives.description: Backers of the deal argue that for the first time, Israel has secured a written framework that officially links its withdrawal to concrete steps by the Lebanese army against Hezbollah. This could, over time, reduce the militia’s grip on southern Lebanon and give Lebanese authorities a legitimate tool to challenge Hezbollah’s weapons.

Skeptics stress that Hezbollah’s instant rejection and its deep entrenchment make the agreement hollow. Without a clear enforcement mechanism and with Hezbollah calling the terms “null and void,” Israeli communities in the north fear a repeat of past failed accords, while opposition politicians see the deal as giving Iran more time to rearm its proxy.

Observers highlight a historical pattern: previous deals like UN Resolution 1701 also demanded Hezbollah’s disarmament but collapsed under similar verification gaps and lack of political will. The success of this framework will depend less on the text and more on whether the Lebanese army can—and wants to—impose authority in areas where Hezbollah is the real power, and whether Iran chooses to block the process.

The two pilot zones are a small-scale test; if they work, the model could be expanded and might reshape the future boundaries of the conflict. However, if Hezbollah re-arms or clashes resume, the half‑implemented deal could become a justification for a new, even larger round of fighting, drawing the U.S. deeper into the region’s tensions.
